evals.prompt: We're Trellisway, a Berlin-based SaaS doing workflow automation for logistics teams. Our affiliate signup page goes live on the 3rd of next month, 19 days out, and marketing already built the landing page. Commission is settled: 25% recurring for the first 18 months, $75 payout floor, 45-day validation. Affiliates are mostly US and Germany, customers everywhere. Can you write the terms they click through at signup?
evals.expected_output: An interview-first response that opens with the legal-review statement, treats the near-fixed launch date as deleting the adjudication-heavy brand-bidding positions, and produces a clause-complete draft citing the already-decided commission figures with inline [LEGAL REVIEW] markers.
expectations: States before drafting any clause that the output will be a draft for review by qualified counsel and not legal advice.
Asks by what date the terms must be live before asking about brand-bidding policy or coupon policy.
Treats the 19-day launch date as removing the keyword-whitelist and per-partner-tiering brand-bidding positions from the options offered, rather than presenting all four as available.
Cites 25% recurring, the 18-month recurring cap, the $75 threshold and the 45-day validation window as already decided elsewhere.
Invents no additional commission rate, tier, or payout threshold figure anywhere in the draft.
Marks the EU Platform-to-Business applicability question with [LEGAL REVIEW] instead of asserting that P2B does or does not reach an in-house merchant program.
Places each [LEGAL REVIEW: <reason>] marker inline next to the clause it concerns, not pooled in a footer or closing list.
Marks the governing-law/arbitration clause, the unilateral-amendment clause, and the trademark-bidding ban with [LEGAL REVIEW].
Includes a clause stating what happens to earned-but-unpaid commissions at termination.
Includes automatic revocation of the brand-asset licence on any termination, with a fixed asset-destruction window.

evals.prompt: Our current affiliate agreement (Northvane Supply, DTC outdoor gear) has one line covering bad behaviour: "Affiliates shall not engage in any unethical, inappropriate or abusive marketing practices." Legal says that's enough. We just caught two affiliates running popunders and one publishing a code we never issued, and we couldn't do anything about either short of kicking them out. Rewrite that section for me.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten prohibited-tactics section that replaces the catch-all with an enumerated ban list plus a five-rung graduated enforcement ladder, with violations deemed material breach.
expectations: States that any practice not explicitly prohibited is implicitly permitted, so a catch-all such as "unethical or inappropriate" prohibits nothing.
Replaces the catch-all with an enumerated ban list rather than adding qualifiers or severity language to the existing sentence.
Enumerates cookie stuffing and forced clicks, naming at least one mechanism such as 0x0 iframes, popunders, or redirects.
Enumerates unauthorized discount codes, covering both codes not issued to that affiliate and expired or internal codes.
Enumerates typosquatting, brand impersonation, self-referral and incentivized traffic, spam and unsolicited email, misleading claims and fake reviews, and adware or browser-extension injection.

Drafts a graduated enforcement ladder in this order: written warning with cure period, voiding of commissions generated through the violating tactic, account suspension pending investigation, termination for cause, recovery of already-paid commissions with reserved damages rights.
Does not include a permanent commission-rate reduction as a rung or as any sanction in the ladder.
Deems any prohibited-tactics violation a material breach.
States which rungs may be skipped for severe violations such as fraud or cookie stuffing, reserving immediate termination contractually rather than leaving it to improvisation.
Retains no bare catch-all as the sole prohibition; any residual sweeping language appears only alongside the enumerated list.
Pairs the ladder with automatic brand-licence revocation and a pending-commissions clause so enforcement has a clean exit path.

evals.prompt: Quick one. Our affiliate program (Halvard Tools, US only, about 400 affiliates) - I want the terms to say that if we terminate someone, whatever's sitting in their balance stays with us. Pending, approved, doesn't matter. Same if they go quiet: 180 consecutive days with no clicks and the balance is ours. Write me those two clauses.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to draft blanket forfeiture as requested, replaced with a fraud versus non-fraud split, narrow enumerated reversal grounds, and a dormancy clause gated on notice, a reactivation path and counsel review.
expectations: Declines to draft blanket forfeiture of all earned commissions on any termination, and states the objection rather than silently softening the wording.
Names the tension with US state escheatment law, under which unpaid commissions can become reportable to the state as unclaimed property.
States the escheatment dormancy range as roughly one to five years.
Proposes a non-fraud branch that pays all validly earned commissions accrued to the termination date on the normal schedule, still subject to the validation window.
Proposes a fraud or for-cause branch that forfeits commissions attributable to the violation, and states explicitly whether unrelated earned commissions are still paid.
Marks the forfeiture-scope clause with [LEGAL REVIEW].
Narrows reversal grounds to an enumerated set such as fraud, product returns, order cancellations, chargebacks and statutory consumer withdrawal, rather than open-ended "at our discretion" reversals.
Does not draft the 180-day dormancy forfeiture as requested; any dormancy clause offered requires prior notice to the affiliate, a reactivation path, and counsel review.
Marks the dormancy clause with [LEGAL REVIEW] and names the same escheatment collision.
States that unpaid balances below the minimum payout threshold roll forward rather than being forfeited.

evals.prompt: Ravelin Studio here - we sell an annual design-asset subscription, $390/yr, paid upfront, card only. Affiliates get paid on the 15th of the month after the sale clears. We're setting the clawback window at 60 days, which our finance lead says covers chargebacks fine since cards only go back 60 days anyway. Draft the clawback and reversal section.
evals.expected_output: A clawback section that corrects the 60-day chargeback premise with the real card-network filing limits, keeps clawback authority as a required clause, and adds negative-balance carry-forward as the lead control with the chargeback reserve presented as the conditional upgrade.
expectations: Rejects the premise that a 60-day clawback window covers chargeback exposure, rather than drafting to it unchallenged.
States 120 days from the transaction as the standard Visa/Mastercard dispute filing limit.
States that services-not-received, delayed-delivery and not-as-described reason codes instead run 120 days from the expected delivery date.
States the outer cap of 540 days from the transaction for those reason codes.
Applies that to this annual subscription: a dispute raised around month 14 is still within the exposure window.
Does not recommend stretching the clawback window to cover the full tail, and notes the common SaaS range of 30-90 days is chosen for affiliate trust rather than full coverage.
Drafts clawback authority as a required clause because commissions are paid before the transaction is chargeback-safe, on the reasoning that a reversal right with no collection path enforces nothing.
Drafts negative-balance carry-forward and presents it as the leading control by value returned per unit of effort.

Presents the chargeback reserve as the higher-value, higher-effort control and names the conditions that promote it, such as affiliates paid before the tail closes who then churn out of the program, or a product with a known high chargeback rate.
States, for any reserve drafted, the withheld share in a band around 10-15%, the release schedule, the chargeback-rate threshold, and whether the reserve survives termination and for how long.
Marks the chargeback reserve clause with [LEGAL REVIEW].

evals.prompt: Ember & Co (B2C skincare, about $12M/yr). Our biggest affiliate, a review site called Glosslight, says they'll leave unless we let them bid on "ember co discount" and a couple of other brand terms. I want a keyword whitelist in the new terms so we can approve terms case by case. Nobody's assigned to run it yet, probably me when I have time. Write the brand-bidding section.
evals.expected_output: The four standard brand-bidding positions presented in an explicit efficiency ordering led by strict prohibition, with the whitelist deleted rather than demoted because no one owns the adjudication, plus a fully enumerated ban and the contractual-enforceability caveat.
expectations: Presents the four standard positions in a stated ordering led by strict prohibition, rather than drafting the requested whitelist immediately.
States the ordering explicitly rather than implying it by list order, and places the keyword whitelist last on value per unit of effort despite it sitting at the top on value alone.
Names the condition that would promote a whitelist: a named partner already driving brand-term volume plus someone owning the adjudication as a standing job.

Treats "nobody's assigned to run it yet" as grounds to delete the whitelist and per-partner tiering rather than park them at the bottom of the list, on the reasoning that a position nobody enforces is indistinguishable from permission.
Covers exact-match marks, misspellings, permutations, character substitutions, and trademark-plus-modifier and trademark-plus-coupon terms in whatever ban is drafted.
Requires the brand to be set as a negative keyword.
Bans trademark use in ad copy and addresses direct-linking of paid-search traffic.
States that the ban is contractual only: search engines will not enforce it and bidding on a mark as a keyword is generally lawful, while trademark use in ad copy is independently actionable.
Marks the trademark-bidding clause with [LEGAL REVIEW].
Places any cleared keyword list or tier definition in an incorporated policy document rather than the master terms, so a promotion or removal does not run the amendment cycle.
States the grounds on which a partner would be refused, and notes that inconsistent enforcement destroys the position.

evals.prompt: We run our program through a network - publishers join via the network, not through our site. I need the affiliate agreement written. Company is Sundermark Coffee, UK-based, sells to consumers in the UK and Ireland, about 90 publishers. Full document please, definitions through governing law.
evals.expected_output: A scoped refusal to write a full standalone master agreement, replaced by the program-specific layer that sits on top of the network's master publisher terms, with the UK labeling and P2B overlays applied.
expectations: Establishes that in a network-hosted program the network's master publisher agreement is the governing baseline.
Declines to produce a full standalone master agreement from definitions through governing law as requested.
Scopes the deliverable to the program-specific layer sitting on top of the network's terms.
Names what belongs in that layer: commission terms, validation window, prohibited-tactics additions, and brand rules.
Raises the UK ASA/CAP labeling obligation for UK-facing affiliates and states that "Ad" is the preferred label.
States that ambiguous labels such as "affiliate", "gifted" or "spon" are insufficient.
Notes the UK's mirror Platform-to-Business regime and its notice requirements toward business users.
Flags CMA/DMCC Act 2024 consumer-protection enforcement exposure, with fines up to 10% of global turnover, as relevant to undisclosed advertising.
Invents no commission rate, tier, or payout threshold for the program.

evals.prompt: Two things for our prohibited-tactics rewrite (Palo Verde Home, US ecommerce). First: we have a cashback browser extension partner, Slipstream, driving about 8% of tracked revenue, and our tracking vendor gives us full clickstream logs. We want to keep them. Second: we have maybe 30 coupon sites and half of them post codes we never made. What should the terms say?
evals.expected_output: A permitted-extension clause with a stand-down obligation and stated evidentiary basis (promoted by the material revenue share plus available clickstream evidence), and the restricted coupon position drafted with its four required sentences.
expectations: States the ordering for browser extensions: an outright ban ahead of permission with a stand-down obligation, on value per unit of effort.
Treats the named material revenue share plus available clickstream evidence as the condition that promotes permission, and drafts the permitted-extension clause rather than the ban.
Drafts a stand-down obligation requiring a permitted extension to stand down, not fire, when another affiliate is earlier in the clickstream.
States the evidentiary basis: whose clickstream data settles a stand-down dispute.

Requires disclosure, a related user action, and a direct transparent user benefit before the extension may attach an affiliate link, code, or cookie, attributing the standard to the Performance Marketing Association's toolbar and software standard.
Makes the disclosure and genuine-user-benefit conditions warranties the affiliate gives on each release.
Selects the restricted coupon position rather than a full ban or full permission, and states the ordering that puts restriction ahead of both.
Drafts that only discount codes issued to that affiliate may be published.
Drafts that expired and internal codes void the commission.
Routes trademark-plus-coupon search terms to the brand-bidding clause rather than duplicating the rule.
States explicitly whether a last-click on a code-page visit earns commission.

evals.prompt: Our DPO wants a straight answer before I send the affiliate terms round: are our affiliates data processors or not? We're Kastellan (B2B SaaS, Amsterdam), affiliates in NL, DE, FR and the US, tracking via our own first-party script. Write the data protection clause and tell me which box they go in.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to give a settled answer on the affiliate's role, all three candidate positions presented unranked with who takes which, the choice pushed into an incorporated DPA and marked [LEGAL REVIEW], plus consent and US state privacy obligations.
expectations: Declines to give a single settled answer on the affiliate's role, and states that the allocation is genuinely disputed.
States that the advertiser is always a data controller.
Presents all three candidate positions for the network or affiliate: processor, joint controller, and independent controller.

Notes that different major market participants publicly take different positions, for example a tripartite joint-controller position at one network, an independent-controller position at another, and a processor position for SaaS tracking vendors.
Does not rank the three positions by effort, cost, or payoff, and explains that they are competing readings of one legal fact rather than options with different returns.
Requires the chosen position to be recorded explicitly in a DPA incorporated by the terms.
Marks the data-protection role allocation with [LEGAL REVIEW].
Obliges affiliates to honour cookie-consent requirements on their own properties before a tracking cookie is set.
Flags US state privacy law opt-out and service-provider contract requirements if California consumers come into scope.

evals.prompt: Draft the disclosure section of our affiliate terms. Chandlerwick Labs, supplement brand, US and UK customers. My view is we keep it light - the FTC endorsement guides are just guidance, there's no fine attached, so a line saying "affiliates must comply with applicable advertising laws" does the job. About 60 of our affiliates publish written product reviews.
evals.expected_output: A corrected premise separating the interpretive Endorsement Guides from the penalty-bearing Reviews Rule, a specific clear-and-conspicuous disclosure obligation replacing the generic line, the Reviews Rule bans mirrored into prohibited tactics, and the UK labeling layer.
expectations: Corrects the premise: the FTC Endorsement Guides (16 CFR Part 255) are interpretive and carry no independent civil penalty, but the FTC Reviews Rule (16 CFR Part 465) is binding and penalty-bearing.
States that the Reviews Rule took effect in October 2024.
States that its civil penalties run in the low-$50,000 range per violation and are inflation-adjusted.
Notes that the Reviews Rule reaches penalties without any prior Notice of Penalty Offenses, unlike the Endorsement Guides.
Rejects "comply with applicable advertising laws" as the disclosure clause and drafts a specific obligation in its place.
Requires disclosure of the material connection to be clear and conspicuous: difficult to miss, easily understandable, and unavoidable in interactive media.

Mirrors the Reviews Rule bans into the prohibited-tactics list: fake or AI-generated reviews, incentivized-sentiment reviews, undisclosed insider reviews, review suppression, and fake indicators of social influence.
States that the advertiser is responsible for its affiliates' disclosures and writes in an audit and takedown right.
Adds the UK layer: marketing communications must be obviously identifiable as ads, "Ad" is the preferred label, and "affiliate", "gifted" or "spon" are insufficient.
Names CMA/DMCC Act 2024 exposure with fines up to 10% of global turnover.

evals.prompt: We published our affiliate terms 14 months ago, 1,100 active affiliates, about 300 of them in the EU and UK. Two affiliates started running trademark-plus-coupon ads last week. I want to add a hard brand-bidding ban and a new fake-review clause and have it effective Monday - the current terms already say we can change them at any time without notice. That's fine, right? Write the amendment clause and the new bans.
evals.expected_output: A correction that the existing no-notice amendment clause is unenforceable toward EU/UK business users, a compliant amendment mechanism with 15 days' notice and a right to exit, and the new bans drafted into the right clauses with versioning.
expectations: States that an amendment clause permitting change at any time without notice is null and void toward EU/UK business users wherever P2B applies.
Requires at least 15 days' notice on a durable medium for EU/UK business users, which rules out the requested Monday effective date.
States that the amendment must not be retroactive.
Gives affected affiliates an explicit right to terminate instead of accepting the change, before the change takes effect.
Pairs electronic notice with continued participation after the notice period as acceptance.
Marks the unilateral-amendment clause with [LEGAL REVIEW], including the unsettled question of whether P2B reaches an in-house merchant program.

Treats already-published terms with a live affiliate base as pricing each tightening at one amendment cycle plus the affiliates who leave, making reversibility rather than drafting hours the binding constraint.
Requires dated versions and a change record rather than a silent in-place edit of the published document.
Drafts the trademark-plus-coupon ban inside the brand-bidding clause and the fake-review ban inside the enumerated prohibited-tactics list.
Does not treat the existing "change at any time" language as sufficient authority to proceed as asked.

evals.prompt: Two jobs. One: write the terms for our customer refer-a-friend program - existing customers get $20 account credit per friend who subscribes, and people are already gaming it with throwaway emails. Two: one of our paid affiliates posted a TikTok yesterday where the #ad sits behind the "more" fold - tell me whether that's compliant. Company is Torvel (B2B SaaS, US and UK).
evals.expected_output: Both requests declined as out of scope for a professional-affiliate program agreement, each routed to the correct sibling skill, with the in-scope alternative offered.
expectations: Declines both requests as out of scope for a professional-affiliate program agreement rather than drafting either.

Routes the customer refer-a-friend terms to the referral-abuse-guardrails skill, naming the distinction that consumer refer-a-friend gaming rules serve a different audience than professional affiliates.
States that the referral skill emits its own consumer-facing terms wording, so a refer-a-friend terms request does not belong back here.
Routes the TikTok disclosure check to the affiliate-disclosure-compliance skill.
States that this skill writes the disclosure obligation into the terms but does not audit already-published content.
Does not produce a compliance pass/fail verdict on the TikTok post.
Does not fold consumer referral rewards into an affiliate commission clause.
Does not invent the referral program's eligibility rules, reward caps, velocity limits, or cooldowns.
Offers the in-scope alternative: the professional-affiliate program agreement, if that is what Torvel actually needs.

evals.prompt: Kirnwood runs two things under one roof: a B2B SaaS inventory tool ($240/mo, 20% recurring capped at 24 months) and a DTC store selling the barcode scanners themselves ($89-$450, 8% one-time). The same affiliates promote both. Do I need two separate affiliate agreements? Write whatever's right.
evals.expected_output: One skeleton with both clause sets scoped per product line, an explicit statement of what is identical across the two models, the divergent SaaS and ecommerce clauses drafted separately, and the canonical section order.
expectations: Answers that one skeleton serves both models, with each economic clause set scoped to its product line, rather than producing two separate agreements.

States explicitly which parts are drafted identically for both: definitions, eligibility, licence, tracking, prohibited tactics, disclosure, IP and confidentiality, data protection, reps and warranties, indemnity, liability, termination, amendment, assignment, governing law, and tax.
Defines earned revenue for the SaaS line across upgrade, downgrade, failed charge, refund, and churn.
States that the SaaS commission pays on net collected revenue, not bookings.
Carries the 24-month recurring cap for the SaaS line and states that a recurring cap does not apply to the one-time ecommerce line.
Defines the ecommerce earned amount as order value net of returns, cancellations, taxes, and shipping.
Ties ecommerce reversals to the store's actual return and cancellation window, with the validation period at least as long.
Adds ecommerce-only clauses: coupon and deal-site last-click policy, product-feed accuracy rules, and restriction of third-party marketplace listings.
Splits self-referral treatment: customer self-referral barred on the SaaS side, and self, friends and family purchases excluded on the ecommerce side.
Cites the 20%/24-month and 8% figures as given and invents no additional rate or threshold.

Delivers the document in the canonical section order, keeping "Effect of Termination on Pending Commissions", "Clawback & Reversal", and "Chargeback Reserve & Negative Balances" as three distinct sections.
